218.title: The creeper (334–337)
218.hook: craving grows like a creeper in a careless person; he leaps like a monkey from tree to tree
218.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions name tanha, craving, as the cause of suffering in the second noble truth; meditators practice noticing craving as it arises, often with a quiet mental label.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekacara, and your line: alone, not lonely. Did you get your hour, and did you enjoy it? Day two hundred eighteen, a new week, and chapter twenty-four: thirst.

If you've ever left a garden alone for one summer, you know what a vine can do. In June it's a little green thread on the fence. By August it has climbed the fence, swallowed a bush, and started up the side of the house. Nobody planted it there on purpose. It just grew, a little every day, while no one was looking. Today a new chapter of the book begins, twenty-six verses long, and it opens with that vine. Today: the creeper.
screen: `A THREAD ON THE FENCE IN JUNE.` → `UP THE HOUSE BY AUGUST.` → `WHILE NO ONE WAS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: The chapter's name, and today's word, is tanha. It means thirst, and in Buddhist teaching it's the name for craving: the restless wanting that the second noble truth calls the cause of suffering. You met it in the Buddha's first sermon. Now the Dhammapada gives it pictures. Verse three hundred thirty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest." Two pictures in one verse. The creeper grows slowly, quietly, wrapping itself around whatever it touches. And the monkey leaps from branch to branch, grabbing one fruit, dropping it, reaching for the next. That's craving from outside and from inside: it spreads, and it never sits still. The next verses say what happens either way. For the one overcome by this thirst, sorrows grow like wild grass after rain. For the one who overcomes it, sorrows fall away like drops of water from a lotus leaf. Notice the word thoughtless, or careless. The creeper grows in a careless person. It's the old theme of the book, heedfulness, from chapter two. The vine doesn't win by force. It wins because nobody's watching the fence. So the first step with tanha isn't to fight it. It's to notice it early, while it's still a thread. Teachers describe three kinds: craving for pleasant things, craving to become something, and craving to be rid of something. All three climb the same way, a little every day.
screen: `TANHA — THIRST, CRAVING.` · `THE CREEPER AND THE MONKEY.` · `WILD GRASS, OR DROPS OFF A LOTUS LEAF.` · `IT GROWS WHERE NO ONE WATCHES.` · then, large: `THE CREEPER GROWS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest with the breath. Now watch, quietly, for the first thread of a wanting. It might be small: wanting to shift position, wanting to check the time, wanting this to be over, wanting a snack later. When one appears, just name it silently: thirst. Don't pull it out, and don't follow it. Watch it climb a little, and watch what happens when you simply see it. Then back to the breath, and wait for the next thread. The bell holds the time.
Tanha. Thirst, craving: the wanting that grows like a creeper and leaps like a monkey.
Your line: the creeper grows. Today, catch one craving while it's still a thread, and just notice it climbing. Day two hundred eighteen.

219.title: Dig up the root (338–343)
219.hook: a tree cut down grows again if the root is sound; so suffering returns while craving lives
219.howItsDone: In Buddhist teaching, craving is uprooted by insight rather than willpower alone; meditators investigate what lies beneath a recurring desire, and teachers often use the verse of the tree that grows back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tanha, thirst, and your line: the creeper grows. Did you catch a craving while it was still a thread? Day two hundred nineteen.

Anyone who has cut down a stubborn bush knows what happens next spring. The stump sits there, looking finished, and then little green shoots come up all around it. You cut them, and they come back. The trunk was never the problem. The roots were still alive under the ground, patient and well fed. It's the same with a habit you thought you'd beaten, a temper you thought you'd outgrown, a worry you thought was gone. Yesterday the creeper. Today, what's underneath it. Today: dig up the root.
screen: `THE STUMP LOOKS FINISHED.` → `SHOOTS COME BACK IN SPRING.` → `THE ROOTS WERE STILL ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred thirty-eight puts it plainly. A tree that's been cut down will grow again, as long as its root is unharmed. In the same way, as long as the craving underneath hasn't been uprooted, suffering keeps coming back, again and again. The verse right before it gave a farmer's picture to go with it. In India, people dig up a tough grass called birana to get at its root, which is fragrant and valuable. We know that root today as vetiver, used in perfumes and cooling mats. So digging up the root isn't only destruction. You dig because what's underneath matters. Then the verses map the roots. They speak of thirty-six streams of craving, all running toward pleasure, and of channels running everywhere, with the creeper sprouting up wherever they reach. When you see the creeper springing up, the text says, cut its root with wisdom. Next comes a picture you can almost see: people driven by thirst run about like a snared hare, held in fetters, suffering again and again. Here's the quiet surprise in these verses. The root isn't the thing you crave. It isn't the phone or the snack or the praise. The root is the craving itself, and the not-seeing that feeds it. That's why the text says to cut it with wisdom, not with force. Chopping the trunk is willpower, and it's useful. Digging the root is understanding why, and that's what stops the shoots in spring.
screen: `CUT DOWN, IT GROWS AGAIN.` · `BIRANA GRASS, FRAGRANT ROOT.` · `THIRTY-SIX STREAMS, THE HARE IN THE SNARE.` · `CUT THE ROOT WITH WISDOM.` · then, large: `DIG THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one craving that keeps coming back for you, the one that sprouts again every spring. Now dig, gently, one layer at a time. What do I want, when I want this? And under that, what do I want? Maybe comfort, or rest, or to feel less alone. Don't force an answer. Just keep asking, softly, and notice whatever comes up. Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mūla. Root: a cut tree grows again while its root lives, so cut craving at the root, with wisdom, not force.
Your line: dig the root. Today, when your recurring craving sprouts, ask once, what am I really wanting? Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: The spider's web (344–350)
220.hook: those caught in passion run down the stream like a spider down the web it spun
220.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the commentary's story of Uggasena the acrobat with verse 348, and use the spider image to show that craving builds its own trap; practice aims to see the web and let it go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mūla, and your line: dig the root. When your craving sprouted, what were you really wanting? Day two hundred twenty.

Watch a spider some morning. It builds the web out of itself, thread by thread, and then it lives there. It runs along the lines it made, back and forth, always on the same paths. The web is its home and its trap at once, and it never looks like a trap from the inside. We do this too. A grudge we've rehearsed for years. A story about who we are. A routine we built to feel safe that now keeps us small. Today's verses hold up the spider. Today: the spider's web.
screen: `THE WEB, SPUN FROM ITSELF.` → `HOME AND TRAP AT ONCE.` → `WEBS WE SPIN.`

segments.voice: These verses start with a man who has left the forest of desire and then runs straight back into it. Look at him, the text says: free, and running back into the chains. Then a surprise about chains. The wise don't call a fetter strong if it's made of iron, wood or rope, the verses say. Far stronger is the grip of longing for jewels, for family, for possessions. It hangs loose, and it's very hard to undo. Then the spider, in verse three hundred forty-seven. Those caught up in passion run down the stream of their desires the way a spider runs down the web it made itself. The key word is itself. Nobody else spun this web. And that's the hopeful part: what you spun, you can step out of. Once they cut it, the verse says, the wise leave the world behind, free of care. The next verse comes with a story from the commentary. It tells of Uggasena, a rich young man who fell in love with an acrobat and became one himself. One day, balanced at the top of a tall bamboo pole in front of a crowd, he heard the Buddha say: let go of what's before, let go of what's behind, let go of what's in between, and cross to the far shore. According to the story, he understood right there on the pole. The chapter ends with the restless mind, tossed by doubt, whose thirst keeps growing, and the calm mind that delights in quieting its thoughts and cuts the fetter. The web is real. So is the edge of it.
screen: `FREE, AND RUNNING BACK.` · `LONGING BINDS HARDER THAN IRON.` · `THE WEB IT MADE ITSELF.` · `UGGASENA ON THE POLE.` · then, large: `STEP OUT OF THE WEB.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Picture a spider's web in the morning light, beaded with dew. Now think of one small web of your own: a story you tell yourself, a grudge, a routine that no longer helps. See the threads you spun. Then, like Uggasena on his pole, let go of what's behind, the past of it, and what's ahead, the worry about it, and even what's in between. Just this breath. Rest here, at the edge of the web. The bell holds the time.
Jāla. A net, a web: we run along webs of desire we spun ourselves, and what we spun, we can step out of.
Your line: step out of the web. Today, leave one small web you spun: skip the old complaint, the old route, the old story, just once. Day two hundred twenty.

221.title: The best gift (351–359)
221.hook: the gift of the dhamma beats all gifts; its taste beats all tastes (Dhammapada 354)
221.howItsDone: Many Buddhists sponsor the printing of dhamma books to give away, and teachers describe the gift of the dhamma (dhamma-dana) as the highest gift; lay people often dedicate the merit of giving to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jāla, and your line: step out of the web. Which small web did you leave? Day two hundred twenty-one, and the end of the chapter on thirst.

Some of the gifts that last aren't things at all. They're sentences someone said at the right moment. A teacher who told you that you were good at something. A grandparent who showed you how to do a thing with your hands. A friend who said, you don't have to carry this alone. The object wears out; the sentence doesn't. The commentary says that today's verse answered a question the gods themselves were arguing about. Today: the best gift.
screen: `GIFTS THAT AREN'T THINGS.` → `OFTEN IT'S A SENTENCE.` → `A QUESTION THE GODS ARGUED.`

segments.voice: The commentary's story goes like this. In the heaven of the thirty-three gods, the devas got into a debate. Which gift is best? Which taste is best? Which delight is best? No one could settle it, so Sakka, their king, came down to ask the Buddha. The answer is verse three hundred fifty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain." Where Müller says the law, the Pali says dhamma: the teaching, the way things truly are. So the best gift is the teaching. Buddhist tradition calls it dhamma-dana, the gift of dhamma, and says it outshines even gifts of food and robes, which are themselves honored. Notice the last line, too. It ties the whole chapter together: the end of thirst, the end of tanha, ends all pain. The creeper, the root, the web, all of it, come undone. The chapter's other verses circle the same place. Tradition places one soon after his awakening, as the Buddha's reply when a wandering ascetic asked who his teacher was: I have conquered all, I know all, and I have no teacher. Another says riches ruin the foolish, but not those who seek the far shore. And the chapter closes with fields: fields are spoiled by weeds, and people are spoiled by passion, hatred, delusion and lust. Gifts given to those free of these weeds, the verses say, bring great reward. The verse doesn't keep the gift of the dhamma for monks. One true teaching, passed on at the right moment, is a small share of it.
screen: `SAKKA'S QUESTION.` · `THE GIFT OF THE DHAMMA EXCEEDS ALL.` · `THE END OF THIRST ENDS ALL PAIN.` · `FIELDS SPOILED BY WEEDS.` · then, large: `THE BEST GIFT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think back over the last few weeks of verses. Which one has stayed with you? The forest, the bigger joy, the elephant bearing the arrow, the creeper, the web? Pick one line. Now think of one person who might need that line right now. Just hold the two together, the verse and the person, and wish them well. You'll decide later whether to share it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhammadāna. The gift of the dhamma, the teaching: it exceeds all gifts, and the end of thirst ends all pain.
Your line: fields are spoiled by weeds. Today, share one teaching that helped you with one person, simply, in your own words. Day two hundred twenty-one.

222.title: Restraint (360–365)
222.hook: restraint in eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, speech and mind is good
222.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, monks walk an alms round each morning, receiving food in silence; lay Buddhists practice sense restraint more lightly, and on holy days many keep eight precepts, including eating only before noon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhammadāna, and your line: fields are spoiled by weeds. Who did you share a teaching with? Day two hundred twenty-two, and chapter twenty-five, the mendicant.

Early morning in a town in Thailand, Laos or Sri Lanka. A line of monks in saffron robes walks slowly down the street, barefoot, eyes lowered, each holding a bowl. People wait on the curb with rice and fruit. The monks don't ask. They don't look around to see what's on offer. They stop, receive, and walk on in silence. Tradition traces the scene to the Buddha's own time, and it's a picture of today's word, and of today's verses. Today: restraint.
screen: `A LINE OF SAFFRON ROBES.` → `BAREFOOT, EYES LOWERED, A BOWL.` → `THEY DON'T ASK.`

segments.voice: Today's word is bhikkhu, a Buddhist monk. A nun is a bhikkhuni. The word comes from bhikkha, alms, so a bhikkhu is literally one who lives on what is given. Max Müller used the Sanskrit form, bhikshu, and titled this chapter for him. The old commentaries add a second meaning, a play on sound: a bhikkhu is one who sees the danger in the round of rebirth. Chapter twenty-five describes the kind of person the word is meant to name, and it starts with the senses. Verse three hundred sixty, in Müller's English: "Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear, in the nose restraint is good, good is restraint in the tongue." The next verse carries the list on: restraint in the body, in speech, in the mind, restraint in all things. The one restrained in all things, it says, is free of all pain. That's the monk on the alms round, eyes lowered, taking what comes. But restraint here isn't a cage. It's the frontier fort from last week, the guard at the gates. The verses go on to describe someone who controls hands and feet and speech, who is collected, content, and happy alone. Then a line about the mouth: the one who speaks wisely and calmly makes the teaching sweet. And a last piece of advice that fits anyone: don't look down on what you've received, and don't envy what others have received. A monk who envies others, the text says, doesn't find stillness. Monks and nuns keep this training full-time. Lay Buddhists keep a lighter version, especially on holy days, when many take extra precepts, like eating only before noon.
screen: `BHIKKHU — ONE WHO LIVES ON ALMS.` · `EYE, EAR, NOSE, TONGUE.` · `BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `DON'T ENVY WHAT OTHERS RECEIVE.` · then, large: `RESTRAINT IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your eyes lower, the way the monks' do on the alms round. Don't close them yet. Just let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you, soft and still. Notice how the mind wants to look up, to see what's around. Let it want. Keep the gaze low. Then close your eyes, and notice the sounds coming in, without reaching out to name them. Receive what comes, like the bowl. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Bhikkhu. A Buddhist monk: one who lives on what is given, restrained in eye, ear, tongue, body, speech and mind.
Your line: restraint is good. Today, restrain one sense for an hour: no music, or no snacks, or eyes off the screens, and notice what the quiet gives back. Day two hundred twenty-two.

223.title: Empty the boat (366–372)
223.hook: empty this boat and it will sail lightly; no meditation without wisdom, no wisdom without meditation
223.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote verse 372 to explain that calm meditation and wisdom are trained together; many meditation traditions pair a practice of stillness with a practice of insight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhikkhu, a monk who lives on what is given, and your line: restraint is good. Which sense did you rest for an hour? Day two hundred twenty-three.

Picture a small wooden boat on a river after a storm. It's riding low, sluggish, barely moving. Water has been coming in all night, and now it sloshes around your ankles. You can row as hard as you like; a boat full of water just won't go. What it needs first isn't more effort. It needs someone to pick up a bucket and start bailing. Most of us row through our days with the boat half full: old worries, old resentments, a list we keep carrying. Today: empty the boat.
screen: `A BOAT RIDING LOW.` → `ROWING HARDER WON'T HELP.` → `PICK UP THE BUCKET.`

segments.voice: The mendicant chapter goes on describing the monk's life. A monk who gets little but doesn't look down on it, one verse says, is praised even by the gods. A monk who lives in kindness, in metta, with faith in the teaching, reaches the place of peace. Then verse three hundred sixty-nine, in Max Müller's English: "O Bhikshu, empty this boat! if emptied, it will go quickly; having cut off passion and hatred thou wilt go to Nirvana." The boat, the old commentators say, is this life, this body and mind. The water is wrong thinking, and especially greed and hatred, seeping in. Bail them out, and the boat rides light and fast toward the far shore. The river and the far shore are old pictures in this tradition. The next verse speaks of the one who has crossed the flood. Then, at the end of this passage, comes one of the most quoted verses in the book. There is no meditation without wisdom, it says, and no wisdom without meditation. The one who has both is close to nirvana. In Pali the two words are jhana, deep meditative absorption, and panna, wisdom or understanding. They need each other. Sitting still without understanding can become a pleasant nap. Understanding without stillness stays in the head, an idea about the boat. Together they're the bucket and the arm that lifts it. So emptying the boat isn't just stopping thoughts. It's seeing clearly what's come in, and letting it go overboard, one bucket at a time.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and imagine yourself in a small boat on a calm river. Feel the water around your ankles: one worry you've been carrying today. Name it, simply. Now picture scooping it up in a bucket and pouring it over the side. Watch it go downstream. If it seeps back in, that's fine; boats leak. Just bail again, gently. Then notice the boat sitting a little higher, and let the breath carry you. The bell holds the time.
Paññā. Wisdom: bail out greed and hatred, and the boat of this life sails lightly, since wisdom and meditation work together.
Your line: one bucket at a time. Today, when one worry sloshes in, bail it out once, name it and let it go downstream. Day two hundred twenty-three.

224.title: The young monk (373–382)
224.hook: rouse yourself by yourself; a young monk who applies himself lights up the world like the moon
224.howItsDone: In several Buddhist countries children may ordain as novices, sometimes for a few weeks or a season; teachers use verse 382 to encourage the young, and verses 379–380 to teach self-reliance in practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paññā, and your line: one bucket at a time. Which worry did you bail out? Day two hundred twenty-four, the end of the week and of the mendicant chapter.

You've probably met someone who does one thing with their whole heart. A kid practicing free throws in the driveway after dark. A cook who tastes the soup six times. A teenager learning a language on their own, just because they love it. There's a brightness about people like that. You notice it across a room. Nobody told them to. They roused themselves. The mendicant chapter ends with exactly that picture: someone young, wholehearted, and shining. Today: the young monk.
screen: `FREE THROWS AFTER DARK.` → `A BRIGHTNESS ACROSS A ROOM.` → `NOBODY TOLD THEM TO.`

segments.voice: The last verses of chapter twenty-five read like advice to a new monk. When you go into an empty room and sit, with a quiet heart, and see the teaching clearly, there's a joy beyond ordinary joys. Watching the body's pieces arise and pass away brings happiness, the text says. Guard the senses, be content, keep good friends. Then a lovely picture: as the jasmine drops its withered flowers, drop greed and hatred. Then the heart of the passage. Rouse yourself by yourself, the text says; examine yourself by yourself. You are your own protector, and your own refuge. Train yourself the way a merchant trains a good horse. And the chapter's last verse, three hundred eighty-two, in Max Müller's English: "He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds." The commentary connects it to a novice named Sumana, still a child, whom the Buddha praised. The point isn't age. It's that you don't have to wait until you're wise, or old, or finished, to shine. You shine by applying yourself, now. You've spent the week on thirst and its way out. The creeper of tanha, and digging up its root. The web you spun, and stepping out of it. The best gift, the teaching. Bhikkhu, and restraint of the senses. The emptied boat. Chapter twenty-five ends with a young monk lighting up the world, and tomorrow the last chapter begins.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For this sit, do one thing wholeheartedly: breathe. Not halfway, while planning dinner. Give each breath your whole attention, the way the kid gives it to the free throw. Feel it begin, feel it fill, feel it turn, feel it leave. When the mind wanders, rouse yourself, by yourself, with no scolding, and come back to the next breath, fresh, like a beginner. You are the young monk here. The bell holds the time.
Dahara. Young: rouse yourself by yourself, since whoever applies themselves wholeheartedly, even young, brightens the world like the moon out of the clouds.
Your line: young and awake. Today, do one ordinary thing wholeheartedly, a dish, a walk, a conversation, like a beginner who loves it. Day two hundred twenty-four.
